clinicalPearls: Characterised by prominent left ventricular trabeculations with deep intertrabecular recesses and a two-layered myocardium of thin compacted and thick non-compacted layers
The clinical triad of concern is heart failure, arrhythmia (including sudden death) and systemic thromboembolism
May present in neonates and children or be discovered incidentally in adults; presentation ranges from asymptomatic to severe cardiomyopathy
Frequently familial with heterogeneous genetics, including sarcomeric gene variants that overlap with hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy
Cardiac MRI is more sensitive than echocardiography for quantifying the non-compacted to compacted myocardial ratio and detecting fibrosis
Anticoagulation is considered when ventricular function is impaired, atrial fibrillation is present, or thrombus is identified, given the risk of embolism from deep recesses
Management otherwise follows standard heart failure and arrhythmia principles, with defibrillator therapy for those at high arrhythmic risk
It can occur in isolation or in association with neuromuscular disorders and congenital heart disease
reference.pathophysiology: Left ventricular non-compaction is thought to reflect arrest of the normal compaction of the trabeculated embryonic myocardium during development, though acquired remodelling may also contribute. The result is a distinctive two-layered ventricular wall with a thin compacted epicardial layer and a thick, heavily trabeculated non-compacted endocardial layer containing deep recesses that communicate with the cavity. This architecture impairs contractile function, promotes microvascular dysfunction and fibrosis, provides a substrate for ventricular arrhythmia, and creates areas of stasis within the recesses that favour thrombus formation and systemic embolism. The genetics overlap with other inherited cardiomyopathies, particularly sarcomeric protein variants.
additionalDifferentials: Prominent normal trabeculation or physiological hypertrabeculation in athletes and pregnancy
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with assessment of the non-compacted to compacted layer ratio
Cardiac MRI for tissue characterisation, late gadolinium enhancement and trabecular quantification
12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia
Assessment of left ventricular systolic function and volumes
Genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives
Evaluation for associated neuromuscular disease when clinically suggested
redFlags: New or worsening heart failure symptoms
Syncope or documented sustained ventricular arrhythmia
Systemic embolic event such as stroke
Family history of cardiomyopathy or premature sudden death
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on ventricular function and arrhythmic burden; incidentally detected cases with preserved function may remain stable, whereas those with impaired systolic function face risks of progressive heart failure, arrhythmia and thromboembolism.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing the condition from prominent trabeculation in athletes or pregnancy on echocardiography alone
Failing to consider anticoagulation in patients with impaired function or atrial fibrillation
Assuming an incidental finding is benign without assessing arrhythmic and thromboembolic risk
Neglecting family screening given the frequently inherited nature
Overlooking associated neuromuscular or congenital conditions
references: ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Treat systolic dysfunction with guideline-directed heart failure therapy including beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (or an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors
Provide oral anticoagulation when systolic function is impaired, atrial fibrillation is present, or intracavitary thrombus is identified, to reduce embolism from the deep recesses
Manage ventricular arrhythmia and assess for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for sudden-death prevention in high-risk patients
Monitor with serial echocardiography or cardiac MRI and ambulatory ECG for progression of dysfunction and arrhythmic burden
Offer genetic testing and cascade screening of first-degree relatives given the frequently familial, sarcomeric basis
Evaluate for an associated neuromuscular disease where clinically suggested
Refer advanced or refractory heart failure for consideration of transplantation or mechanical circulatory support
